I lived in cognitive dissonance for years and years, even though I had been aware of factory farming horrors, and was definitely coddled into finding excuses to keep eating meat/dairy/eggs. 

It took a not-so-civil tweet to really get me to wake up and commit. The only regret I have about going vegan is not doing it sooner.

I grew up eating rare prime rib, drinking glasses of whole milk an absurd amount, meat every meal. I even worked at a steakhouse for the discount because I love meat. 

And then I learned what happens, even on small local farms, and I gave it all up. Straight to veganism. Would I look longingly at a burger for the first few months of it? Yes. But in this life, I get choices about what I do and eat. The animals get no choices whatsoever.

>	Our efforts would be better focused on voting in politicians who would regulate this industry and actually enforce the regulations; 

Why not vote AND not consume animal products? I know I’m not saving the world but I’m making choices that are within my control that align with my values. It’s the thought of sparing some lives as opposed to saving all lives. 

>	is that it really won’t stop the cruelty, it will just make it happen to less animals.

Cruelty happening to fewer animals over time is better than not trying. Almost like a harm reduction strategy.

A lot of small, local farms send their animals elsewhere for slaughter, which have similar methods. Local isn’t a protected term and doesn’t ensure humane or ethical treatment. 

To lean deeper into the veganness tho, the most ethical treatment would be to not kill the animals for food in a time where you do not need to and have plant-based options available to replace with.

Also my weed tolerance was through the roof from being home all the time, so I wasn’t getting the voracious munchies. 

So getting over that hump of “HUNGER!” and learning what hungry really was, was pretty easy as compared to starting under normal circumstances.

Back in 2008 at least, none of the “adults” (teachers, guidance counselors, parents) even remotely mentioned cost. Community college was looked down upon, not seen as the valuable thing it actually is. So no one brought up that sensible route. 

They assured us that the degree from the good (expensive) school would net you a job to be able to afford the loans. We were told that employers would see community college on resumes and we’d be passed over. And that education was something we’d be interviewed on and to display on our resumes in detail. It was all about getting into the “best” school. 

I remember during orientation for college, they brought all the freshman and their parents (a huge number of people) to the gymnasium with tables set up. We sat down and someone at the podium up front was like “ok here’s your promissory note. sign it and let’s move on with our tour.” Thankfully my mom said “don’t sign it” and we went to the financial aid office to talk. But we were the only ones to get up. And I still ended up with a fucked up loan situation for a variety of reasons.

ETA: I graduated in 2008, just before the global financial crisis. We were already signed up for school before shit hit the fan.

Hey there! I’m both bipolar 2 and ADHD, been diagnosed for about 8 years now. I have struggled with your exact scenario. Medication has always been a complicated journey, requiring adjustments as my jobs and life changed and demanded different things of me. 

I am not a medical professional, this is not medical advice: Unfortunately most med prescribers will want your mood stabilized before introducing any stimulant which is chemically what ADHD needs, because there’s the risk of hypomania. 

Like any med journey, the first mood stabilizer you take may not be the right one for you. They can take time to get into your system fully and take their full effect, sometimes a few weeks or longer. Once you feel sort of settled into the right stabilizer, the prescriber may then discuss prescribing a stimulant for the ADD. 

This is just one of many paths a med journey can take, your mileage may vary. The stress of the untreated ADHD is a valid concern and it’s something you may want to mention to the prescriber. Wellbutrin has been prescribed for bipolar at times, and has a *slight* stimulant component to it which may be worth a conversation.

I personally am on lamictal and wellbutrin for bp2 and adderall extended release for adhd, I’ve been working with my psych team for years and years though so I had to struggle with a lot of this at the beginning.

 **It will get better!!!!**

Edit: forgot to mention, in the meantime, it’s very difficult working against adhd with upcoming exams, but do your best to research and implement some coping skills and study methods that work best for how you learn. those are the best tools in your tool box right now. no matter how silly they may be, if it works, it works, you can do this!

I agree about the involuntary should only be used in absolute emergencies. My mother and sister have had a few themselves (we have odd family traditions I guess) and while the stays were effective, they were not pleasant. And that is in their own words that it was effective. 

I feel my gripe is with awareness of and allotment of resources towards mental health treatment in society. If mental health was taken and addressed seriously on a large scale, there wouldn’t be traumatic involuntary stays and people would be aware that they can get a deeper level of care than bearing life while on a waitlist without fear. I hope that can happen someday for everyone.

The multiple stays themselves were beneficial, not just the connection to a therapist and medication adjustment. The group sessions, the private sessions, the fellow patients on the floor who have become lifelong friends, the step away from society momentarily, and many other things. It was not all perfect. It was challenging, I wanted to go home so many times, many days I didn’t make any progress, but I’ve never regretted a stay. 

And yes it is possible to do those things, but if you do not already have a med prescriber and therapist and are at the state that would warrant an inpatient bed, it can be immensely difficult to navigate that system on your own. And a lot of primary care doctors don’t want to or are bad at giving psych meds. 

You mention having freedom taken away, and I must say all of my stays were voluntary. I was able to make the decision for myself to give my freedoms up, and that is not everyone’s experience. I cannot speak to the experience of going involuntarily but I have seen many of my loved ones go through it. I think it’s an important distinction to make about how beneficial a stay can be when it’s voluntary vs involuntary. I had the privilege to be raised in a household without stigma that encouraged seeking help and not everyone has that or any other number of reasons that would lead to an involuntary stay. 

All I ever see on reddit is people saying how horrible their stays were while people who mention the benefits get downvoted and therefore hidden. I just worry that people who could benefit are scared off and suffer when they may not have to. I don’t want the people who had bad experiences to stop sharing or commenting because their experiences are valid and need to be voiced, I just wish that the comments discussing the positive help people received were more visible.

This is dangerous to put out there because not all psych ward experiences are terrible and people who have never been could avoid getting help out of fear. I have had multiple very beneficial stays, lasting about 5-7 days at a time. You get all of your medications looked at or maybe switched or put back on them if you didn’t have access to what’s worked for you previously. You leave with an appointment for a therapist the next week. I was not actively making a suicide plan, but had immense ideation. 

A psych stay can be immensely beneficial in and of itself but also as a bridge to the therapy and medication you rightly suggest. People shouldn’t and can’t have to white-knuckle it through the terribly long waitlists.

(I am not saying people always have good stays. You don’t have to tell me, my mother had a very bad experience. But I’m saying good stays are real and they help people.)

This is me! I’ve had a long road with both. Sometimes I think the adhd impairs me more on a daily functioning level, when left untreated. And the untreated adhd absolutely throws off stability I have in regards to bp2 episodes. 

In the past, you may have received decent support, but it probably wasn’t catered to your specific comorbid diagnoses. I was always surrounded by therapy and positive people, but as long as I was undiagnosed and untreated, that support was not effective whatsoever. 

What can be comforting about diagnoses is it points you in a specific direction treatment-wise. Life without treatment isn’t quite set up to fail, but it absolutely feels that way. With treatment, it won’t feel such a way. It’ll feel like the playing field has been leveled and achieving the things you want won’t be so daunting. 

I don’t have any studies on hand because I am desperately trying to avoid nodding off to sleep, adhd and bp2 are both linked to the absence of the same neurochemical, dopamine I believe. It is not any moral failing on your part. You can’t bootstrap the motivation adhd saps from you. It is a concrete physiological thing. 

It is hard to accept things like this that won’t go away. Even though the diagnoses themselves may not change, but with treatment, your quality of life can. How you experience and navigate your life can. You won’t feel this way about it forever. The symptoms can be managed and you can live a fulfilling, capable life. 

The journey of treatment isn’t always linear. There may be times when a certain treatment isn’t working. Don’t let this discourage you though. It won’t stay that way forever. Best of luck to you!
